doc.title: Bob Stewart interviewed by Monk Rowe, Rome, New York, August 24, 2006

title: Many hats, including the Collective Black Artists Big Band
summary: Stewart describes his varied hats, notably dashiki-era Collective Black Artists Big Band under Reggie Workman and the Strata East label.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums

blocks.x: Well it’s been to my benefit to have so many hats in a certain kind of way, from Dixieland straw hat to a hat that matches with a dashiki, to you know, and all the different varieties in between.
Who did you have a dashiki with?

This was early in New York in the late sixties, early seventies, when the call for dress in a lot of the jazz bands during that period that weren’t necessarily in the mainstream was dashiki, and this particular band was Collective Black Artists Big Band. And it was a big band that was under the auspices of Reggie Workman and people like Buster Williams and sometimes Kenny Dorham came in and sat in with the band and Frank Foster was there and Charlie Persip, drummer. And this was an organization that was the beginnings in New York of musicians sponsoring themselves. They created their own record company, Strata East and they recorded the big band and recorded other artists on the Strata East label rather than waiting for some record company to decide to bless them with the possibility of recording an album.
